Q3 GDP revision shows the economy was even stronger coming into the fourth quarter than previously thought.

Q3 GDP revised up well more than expected to 4.3% (est 3.5%; advance 3.4%), the fastest pace since Q3 2023. The 0.9-point upgrade was the biggest advance-to-second-estimate revision since Q2 2020, and since Q2 2015 excluding the pandemic.

▪️ Investment drove about half of the upgrade, led by software. Software spending grew 22.3% instead of 9.6% after BEA revised software prices to a 7.0% annualized decline from a 1.6% rise.
▪️ Information processing equipment added 0.95 point to growth, a record in data back to 1947.
▪️ Consumer spending was revised up to 4.2% (est 3.9%; advance 3.8%), the fastest since Q4 2024. Goods were revised up (pharmaceuticals, software, gasoline) and services down, with health care growth cut to 1.3% from 4.9%.
▪️ Final sales to private domestic purchasers were revised up to 5.8%, the most since Q2 2021.
▪️ Trade was still a big drag, with net exports subtracting 3.2 points, the most since Q1 2025.
▪️ The GDP price index was revised down to 1.9% (est 2.3%). PCE prices (2.1%) and core PCE (2.5%, in line) were unrevised.
▪️ Real GDI rose 4.4%, slightly faster than GDP, and the average of the two was also 4.4%, the most since Q4 2023.
▪️ Corporate profits rose $206B to a record $4.92T, up 21.3% from a year ago and a record 14.9% of GDP in data back to 1947. Nonfinancial profit margins were the highest since 1955.
▪️ The saving rate was revised down to 3.9%, the lowest since Q3 2022.

Prices:
▪️ Core +0.29% m/m (est 0.3%); 3.26% y/y (est 3.2%), the highest since November 2023.
▪️ Headline +0.32% (est 0.3%); 3.845% y/y (est 3.8%), the highest since May 2023.

▪️ Energy price index at another record high; gasoline +38.02% y/y.
▪️ Share of 244 components up more than 3% y/y rose to 51.2% from 48.4%, vs the 32% pre-pandemic average Warsh cited.

Incomes:
▪️ Personal income +0.73% (est 0.4%), the most since April 2025, helped by a one-time Medicare premium rebate.
▪️ Real disposable income +0.51%, the most since January.

Spending:

So inflation is re-accelerating while real spending stalls, and households saved a Medicare rebate rather than spending it.

Monday's rip on Jensen Huang's return gave the S&P 500 its best day since April 2025, but a lot of that buying wasn't anyone's decision. Per Nomura's Charlie McElligott (via ZeroHedge), a lot was mechanical:

▪️ Leveraged ETFs were projected to buy $41B into the close, second only to the April 9, 2025 tariff-pause day ($46.5B) in data back to 2006.
▪️ CTAs, at max short, had to cover ~$16B of S&P futures on a close above 7,043 (up to $34B globally).
▪️ Dealers bought back hedges as the VIX collapsed.
▪️ Only vol control sold ($10B–$16B).

The catch is that those buyers are now done. Covering only got CTAs back to flat, and Nomura's model doesn't have them buying to go long until 7,625, 5.9% above Tuesday's 7,201 close. Vol control sells any 1%+ move in either direction. So the next leg needs discretionary buyers, and Goldman's Peter Callahan said Monday looked more like "net exposure management" than "investing."

And credit never bought it. Goldman's Rich Privorotsky said if Nvidia rallied while neocloud spreads stayed under pressure, "we're probably just covering shorts." Tuesday:
▪️ Goldman's IG CDS basket hit its widest since spring 2025.
▪️ HY CDX topped 385bp.
▪️ Goldman's hyperscaler CDS basket hit a record.
▪️ CoreWeave bonds hit record lows (Bloomberg).

Semis gave back nearly two-thirds of Monday's 14% (SOX −7.9%). That 5.9-point lag versus the Nasdaq-100 is close to the October 2000 record (6.9 points), in Bloomberg data shared by Goldman.

The bull case: Privorotsky says if the market can "sit still for a couple of days," systematic funds can re-lever into year-end. But near term the mechanical bid is spent.

@CarsonResearch recently published the 25 biggest up days of the last 20 years and what followed. We rebuilt that table from the raw index data and split it the same way we did yesterday. The table below separates the days that came with a recession, a credit event, or an earnings contraction from those that did not.

Two things stand out. 

1) Big up days are mostly bear-market events. Only two of the 24 prior cases, December 2018 and April 2025, came with clean fundamentals. The other 22 clustered in 2008, 2009, 2020, and the euro debt scares. 

2) The 12-month averages also look similar, but the paths don’t. 
- With fundamentals intact, the index was higher a month later both times and averaged 28.8% over the next year. 
- With weak fundamentals, it was higher only half the time a month later, and the worst three-month return was a 23.6% loss. 

Fundamentals decide where the market ends up a year from now, but they don’t make the next few weeks any smoother. Even the two clean cases were lower a week later. In April 2025, the index gave back 3.5% the very next day, exactly what we are seeing over the last two days.

The S&P 500 hit a reading Friday that Bespoke Investment Group dubbed "apocalyptically oversold": 4.1 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average, per the WSJ's Spencer Jakab.

It's happened only five other times since the 1960s, and the S&P was higher a year later every time, by an average of 19.4%. That's more than double the 8.9% average for all one-year periods since 1960:

▪️ Nov 22, 1963 (JFK assassination): next day +4.0%, one year later +23.2%.
▪️ Oct 19, 1987 (Black Monday): next day +5.3%, one year later +22.9%.
▪️ Aug 6, 1990 (Iraq invades Kuwait): next day +0.1%, one year later +15.1%.
▪️ Aug 8, 2011 (U.S. downgrade): next day +4.7%, one year later +25.2%.
▪️ Aug 21, 2015 (China slowdown, oil slump): next day −3.9%, one year later +10.7%.

In 1963, 1987 and 2011, the signal day's close was at or within 2% of the low for the next year.

But Jakab flags the catch: four of the five came after a single shock, leaving a big wall of worry to climb as things normalized. The only one driven by general market jitters, 2015, had the weakest rebound. The S&P fell another 7.2% into the February 2016 low and was still down 2.5% six months out. He thinks the AI selloff looks more like 2015.

Bottom line: the signal's record argues against panic, but with only five cases, and this one looking more like 2015 than a one-off shock, we might expect a choppier path than the 19% average suggests.

I'll give Deutsche Bank credit for being aggressive. While some strategists were trimming their targets during the selloff, Deutsche set its 2027 S&P 500 target at a street high 9,000 over the weekend (MarketWatch). That's compared to the current median target of 8,700.

At the time, the team, led by Jim Reid, thought last week's selloff had further to go before bottoming, but said earnings should keep losses in check. They say AI "could deliver the productivity breakthrough," but also warn that the investment needed to get there creates "the possibility of overinvestment."

The math on 9,000:
▪️ It's 30.2% above Friday's close of 6,910.39 and 15.1% above the October 6 record of 7,818.93.
▪️ On DB's reported 2027 EPS estimate of $430, 9,000 is about 20.9x earnings. Yardeni puts Friday's forward P/E at 16.4x, the lowest since the 2022 bear market. So this is as much a bet that valuations rise again as a bet on earnings.

I checked every time since 1954 that the S&P first closed 10%+ below a record (a correction). Friday was the 25th. Here's what it did over the next ~13.4 months, the same window DB's target covers:
▪️ It was higher 16 of 24 times, with a median change of +10.9%. From Friday's close, that's about 7,660.
▪️ It gained 30%+ only twice: 1997 (+35%) and 2020 (+38%).
▪️ 11 of the 24 became bear markets. The other 13 had a median gain of +15.7%, which works out to about 8,000.

DB's 2025 target of 7,000 was within about 2% of the actual 6,845.50 finish. Its 2026 target of 8,000 was also the Street high, and it now needs a 15.8% rally in under six weeks.

Definitely not off the table. Valuations have reset hard, and UBS makes the same argument for its 8,900. 1997 and 2020 show a rebound this big can happen. But history makes 9,000 a best case, not a base case. The typical outcome is getting back to around the old high by the end of 2027, and almost half of these corrections got worse first.

The Fed's last scheduled speaker before the blackout may have changed the debate.

New York's Williams, the FOMC vice chair and the clearest voice of the committee's center (which also includes Powell, Jefferson and most likely Warsh), told reporters Monday: "I would not exclude, you know, moving at consecutive meetings at all if that was what was needed." If the economy stays strong and inflation pressures don't ease, "you wouldn't just want to wait around" (Reuters).

That's a marked contrast with his comments as recently as Sept. 29, when he suggested policymakers probably only needed to deliver one more rate hike this year, and said, "With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency."

It also comes three days after Philadelphia's Paulson, one of the committee's most dovish members, who as recently as Nov. 10 called for "further gradual tightening," called back-to-back hikes "a very reasonable thing to have on the table."

Add Waller, Hammack, Logan, Cook, Musalem and Goolsbee, who've already talked about the need for a quicker pace, and a January hike is now squarely in play.

With a 25bp December hike fully priced, the question for Dec. 9 is whether the quicker-pace group gets a signal that a January hike is coming. What makes that difficult:

▪ Chair Warsh has stepped almost entirely away from guidance on rates, and the statement has been shortened. October's only forward-looking line: "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
▪ The dot plot shows where officials see rates at the end of 2027, not the path in between.

Markets already lean toward January, pricing 42 basis points of tightening through that meeting, or about two-thirds of a hike on top of December's quarter point (CME FedWatch).

Wednesday is packed with economic data ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

The most notable US economic data is October’s personal income and spending report, which includes core PCE inflation, the Fed’s preferred inflation metric. Bloomberg consensus is for core PCE to rise 0.3% m/m (3.2% y/y, from 3.1%) and headline PCE 0.3% (3.8% y/y, from 3.6%). J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs both expect core at 0.29%. Personal income and spending are both expected to rise 0.4%.

The second estimate of Q3 GDP comes at the same time (which should also include Gross Domestic Income, another key economic indicator), with consensus at 3.5% (the advance estimate was 3.4%), while J.P. Morgan and Goldman both expect 3.7%. We’ll also get October durable goods orders (consensus +0.5%) and new home sales (650,000), plus weekly jobless claims a day early because of the holiday (consensus 200,000).

The Fed releases its Beige Book at 2pm ET, its last major release before the December 8-9 FOMC meeting. As I mentioned in the Week Ahead: “The Beige Book is important…as the Fed pays a lot of attention to anecdotal ‘on the ground’ reports like that one.” As noted yesterday, there are no scheduled Fed speakers until the meeting.

Non-Bill (>1yr in maturity) US Treasury auctions include $44B of 7-year notes at 11:30am ET, earlier than usual ahead of the holiday.

Deere ($DE) is the only S&P 500 component reporting earnings, before the open.

Ex-US highlights include Australia’s October CPI (7:30pm ET Tuesday), Japan’s October services PPI (6:50pm ET Tuesday) and final machine tool orders, Germany’s final Q3 GDP (2am ET) and French consumer confidence for November (2:45am ET). The ECB Governing Council holds a non-monetary policy meeting in Frankfurt, EU and Western Balkan leaders meet for a summit in Brussels and the OECD and African Union hold their International Economic Forum on Africa in Paris.

@C_Barraud's Tuesday Morning Brief noted the eurozone flash PMIs in back-to-back-to-back posts for the eurozone, then Germany and France, and the results were striking. A steady eurozone headline hides a K-shaped eurozone: Germany is booming while France slides deeper into contraction.

▪️ The eurozone composite PMI held at 51.7, a fifth straight month of growth. S&P Global's Chris Williamson says that's consistent with the economy growing at a near 0.3% pace in Q4. Manufacturing rose to 52.9, a two-month high, while services slipped to 51.2, a five-month low.
▪️ Germany's composite PMI jumped to 55.0 from 53.4, its highest since March 2022. Manufacturing output hit 57.4, a 63-month high, and services rose to 54.0, a 13-month high. New business rose at the steepest pace in more than four and a half years. Factories added workers for the first time in nearly three and a half years, ending the longest run of manufacturing job cuts in the survey's history.
▪️ France's composite fell to 46.2 from 46.6, a six-month low and a second straight month of contraction. Manufacturing output plunged to 44.5, a 21-month low, as factory production fell at the fastest pace since February 2025. Excluding the pandemic, French firms' outlook for the year ahead is the gloomiest since late 2012. S&P's Joe Hayes says the data have "raised the odds of France entering a technical recession" in Q4.
▪️ That leaves an 8.8-point gap between the two composites. S&P says Germany's outperformance over France is the greatest in six years. Growth in the rest of the eurozone was modest and the slowest in six months.

Germany's factories are riding a wave of defense and AI-related investment on top of massive government spending. France is weighed down by budget fears and next year's presidential election, while social unrest and the high cost of living hit consumer-facing services across the region.

Price pressures eased but stayed elevated. Input costs rose at a three-month low and selling prices at the slowest pace since August, with French firms raising their prices at the slowest pace in eight months. Williamson still calls the surveys "a clear hawkish signal," with inflation running well above the ECB's 2% target. Bloomberg Economics says the data should keep the ECB on track for another hike in December, which would be its third this year.

That's the eurozone's classic one-size-fits-all problem. With eurozone inflation at 4% (per Bloomberg), rate hikes hit France, which is already flirting with recession, just as hard as Germany, whose boom is fueled by fiscal spending that higher rates do little to slow. That may help explain why overall business optimism has fallen four months in a row to the lowest since May.

After a solid 2-year Treasury auction Monday, which saw an improvement in indirect demand, today’s $70 billion 5-year auction was back to the pattern of the auctions earlier this month, with weak indirect demand (which includes foreign buyers), in this case dropping to the least since March 2020.

Still, record direct demand helped lift overall demand to the best since August, but the auction nevertheless ended in the 13th straight tail (yield above expectations), which ZeroHedge calls the longest such stretch on record.

The details:

▪️ Indirect: 54.3%, lowest since March 2020, vs. 60.0% in October and a 61.9% six-month average.

▪️ Direct: 36.7%, a record since bidder data began in 2008, vs. 29.4% in October and a 25.5% six-month average (prior high: 31.7%, December 2025).

▪️ Dealers: 9.0%, lowest since December 2025, vs. 10.6% in October and a 12.6% six-month average.

▪️ Bid-to-cover: 2.37, highest since August, vs. 2.33 in October and a 2.31 six-month average.

▪️ Tail: +0.3 basis point (4.719% high yield vs. 4.716% when-issued), vs. +0.4 in October and a +0.9 six-month average.

▪️ High yield: 4.719%, lowest since August, vs. 4.845% in October and a 4.510% six-month average.

ZeroHedge called it “a very ugly 5Y auction,” saying “the internals were a mess.” That seems a little dramatic, as there’s nothing surprising about this auction tailing (it's the 13th in a row), and the shift from indirect to direct demand may reflect a change in how buyers are categorized more than anything. Still, it was the 10th straight note or bond auction with the indirect share below its six-month average.

Wednesday’s 7-year will wrap up the month.
